claims.quote: My method of lessening the consumption of steam, and consequently fuel, in fire engines, consists of the following principles:

That vessel in which the powers of steam are to be employed to work the engine, which is called the cylinder in common fire engines, and which I call the steam vessel, must, during the whole time the engine is at work, be kept as hot as the steam that enters it;
first, by enclosing it in a case of wood, or any other materials that transmit heat slowly;
secondly, by surrounding it with steam or other heated bodies;
thirdly, by suffering neither water nor any other substance colder than the steam to enter or touch it during that time.

In engines that are to be worked wholly or partially by condensation of steam, the steam is to be condensed in vessels distinct from the steam vessels or cylinders, although occasionally communicating with them; these vessels I call condensers;
whilst the engines are working, these condensers ought at least to be kept as cold as the air in the neighborhood of the engines, by application of water or other cold bodies.

Whatever air or other elastic vapor is not condensed by the cold of the condenser, and may impede the working of the engine, is to be drawn out of the steam vessels or condensers by means of pumps, wrought by the engines themselves, or otherwise.

I intend in many cases to employ the expansive force of steam to press on the pistons, or whatever may be used instead of them, in the same manner in which the pressure of the atmosphere is now employed in common fire engines.
In cases where cold water cannot be had in plenty, the engines may be wrought by this force of steam only, by discharging the steam into the air after it has done its office

I intend in some cases to apply a degree of cold not capable of reducing the steam to water, but of contracting it considerably, so that the engines shall be worked by the alternate expansion and contraction of the steam.

Instead of using water to render the pistons and other parts of the engine air and steam tight, I employ oils, wax, resinous bodies, fat of animals, quick-silver and other metals in their fluid state.
The fifth claim was for a rotary engine, and need not be quoted here.

components.label: Steam vessel
components.sourceTerm: steam vessel (called the cylinder in common fire engines)
components.role: Works the engine by the powers of steam; to be kept as hot as the steam entering it while the engine works.

components.label: Slow-conducting case
components.sourceTerm: a case of wood, or any other materials that transmit heat slowly
components.role: Encloses the steam vessel; its materials transmit heat slowly.

components.label: Steam or heated surround
components.role: Surrounds the steam vessel to keep it hot.

components.label: Condenser
components.role: Vessel distinct from the steam vessel, occasionally communicating with it, in which the steam is condensed.

components.label: Applied cold water or bodies
components.role: Keeps the condensers at least as cold as the surrounding air while the engine works.

components.label: Extraction pumps
components.sourceTerm: pumps, wrought by the engines themselves, or otherwise
components.role: Draw uncondensed air or elastic vapor out of the steam vessels or condensers.

components.label: Piston
components.sourceTerm: pistons, or whatever may be used instead of them
components.role: Pressed by the expansive force of steam in place of atmospheric pressure; made tight without water.

components.label: Fluid sealing materials
components.sourceTerm: oils, wax, resinous bodies, fat of animals, quick-silver and other metals in their fluid state
components.role: Make pistons and other parts air and steam tight instead of water.

functions.label: Keep the steam vessel as hot as its steam
functions.statement: Maintain the steam vessel at the heat of the entering steam throughout operation, using a slow-conducting case, a heated surround and exclusion of colder substances.

functions.label: Condense steam in a separate vessel
functions.statement: Condense the steam in condensers distinct from the steam vessel, which communicate with it only occasionally.

functions.label: Keep the condenser cold
functions.statement: While the engine works, keep the condensers at least as cold as the nearby air by applying water or other cold bodies.

functions.label: Remove uncondensed air and vapor
functions.statement: Pump out air or other elastic vapor that the condenser does not condense and that may impede the engine.

functions.label: Press the piston with expansive steam
functions.statement: Use the expansive force of steam to press on the pistons, in the way atmospheric pressure is used in common fire engines.

functions.label: Work by steam force alone
functions.statement: Where cold water is scarce, work the engine by the force of steam only, discharging the steam into the air after use.

functions.label: Work by alternate expansion and contraction
functions.statement: Apply a degree of cold that contracts the steam without reducing it to water, so the engine works by alternate expansion and contraction.
functions.componentNote: The quoted passage names no vessel or part for this principle.

functions.label: Seal with fluid materials instead of water
functions.statement: Make pistons and other parts air and steam tight with oils, wax, resinous bodies, animal fat, quicksilver or other fluid metals instead of water.
